analysis.one_liner: Bars serious labor-law violators from federal food contracts and meat inspections for five years.
analysis.headline: The bill never received a hearing or a vote; it died in the House Agriculture Committee with 37 Democratic cosponsors and no Republican support.
analysis.plain_summary: The federal government buys enormous amounts of meat and poultry, and every plant it buys from must pass federal inspection to sell its product at all. This bill would require any company holding a Department of Agriculture contract to disclose each year whether it or its subcontractors were found in the past three years to have violated labor laws — including child labor, wage, and safety rules. Companies with serious, repeated, or pervasive violations could be barred from USDA contracts, and from federal meat and poultry inspection, for five years, unless they completed negotiated corrective measures. Knowingly hiding violations would be a crime.
analysis.who_benefits: Workers at meat and poultry plants and their contractors — including the minors who in recent years have been found working overnight sanitation shifts — would gain real enforcement leverage, since a violator's access to federal contracts and to legal meat sales would be at risk. Companies that follow labor law would also benefit from facing competitors held to the same rules.
analysis.who_benefits_short: Meatplant and sanitation workers, including child workers

how_it_helps.text: Any USDA contractor would have to disclose annually whether it or a subcontractor received an adverse administrative determination, arbitral award, or civil judgment for violating listed labor laws in the prior three years, including the Fair Labor Standards Act (which contains the child labor provisions), workplace safety law, wage laws, and H-2A farmworker protections.
The Labor Department could negotiate corrective measures with a disclosing company, giving violators a path to fix problems and stay off the ineligible list.

Each year, Labor would send USDA a list of entities with serious, repeated, or pervasive violations or with uncompleted corrective measures; USDA could not solicit contracts from them or conduct federal meat and poultry inspections at their facilities for five years — and a plant cannot legally sell meat or poultry without federal inspection.
Knowingly failing to make the required disclosure would be a federal crime, with contract payments treated as the loss to the government.

analysis.who_pays: Meat and poultry processors and their contractors — particularly sanitation and staffing subcontractors — would bear the cost of disclosure and would lose contracts, and potentially federal inspection, if they were serious or repeat violators. Workers at a plant that lost inspection could lose their jobs with it.
analysis.who_pays_short: Meat and poultry contractors with labor violations

drawbacks.text: The harshest tool in the bill is the five-year inspection ban, which effectively closes a plant; that penalty would fall partly on the plant's own workers, who lose their jobs alongside the violator.

The disclosure requirement covers an unusually broad list of laws — from civil rights and disability discrimination statutes to pesticide worker-protection rules — and a Labor Department list based on 'serious, repeated, or pervasive' violations would involve judgment calls that contractors could contest, creating uncertainty for companies and their lenders.
Compliance costs would fall hardest on smaller contractors and subcontractors, who would need systems to collect labor-violation records across their supply chains.

analysis.benefit_vs_cost: The bill uses the government's purchasing power and its control of meat inspection as enforcement leverage, which is a far stronger tool than fines alone, and the corrective-measure process gives violators an off-ramp short of the five-year ban. The inspection ban is genuinely severe — it shuts a plant down — and that cost lands on plant workers as well as the violator, which is the strongest good-faith objection. On balance the bill is a targeted accountability measure aimed at companies repeatedly breaking child labor and wage laws, not at the industry as a whole.

outcome.mechanism: It was referred to the House Agriculture Committee the day it was introduced, and the committee never took it up — no hearing, no markup, no vote — before the Congress ended.

narrative.text: Rep. Greg Casar introduced the Child Labor Exploitation Accountability Act on April 25, 2023, and it was referred to the House Committee on Agriculture.
Thirty-seven House Democrats cosponsored the bill; no Republican did.

The complete action history shows only the introduction and the committee referral; the House Agriculture Committee never scheduled a markup or floor action, and the bill died there when the 118th Congress ended on January 3, 2025.

outcome.who_came_out_ahead: Meat and poultry contractors and their subcontractors that violate labor laws keep their access to USDA contracts and federal inspection without any new disclosure duty, and the workers they employ — including any minors — keep the status quo enforcement regime. Companies that already comply with labor law gain nothing.

for.name: Rep. Greg Casar
for.what_they_did: Introduced the bill and recruited 37 Democratic cosponsors.

against.name: House Agriculture Committee
against.role: Committee of referral (Republican majority in the 118th Congress)
against.what_they_did: Never scheduled a hearing, markup, or vote on the bill after receiving the referral on the day of introduction.

sides.party_line_note: All 38 sponsors and cosponsors were House Democrats; no Republican signed on, and the bill sat in a committee chaired by the Republican majority until the Congress ended.

industries.note: Federal inspection is a legal precondition for selling meat or poultry, so a five-year inspection bar is effectively a plant shutdown, and loss of USDA contracts cuts off a major buyer. Only companies with serious, repeated, or pervasive labor violations — including child labor — would face that penalty, and the bill's whole point is to make violations costly.

These firms are often the direct employers of overnight cleaning crews, where recent child labor cases have arisen; they would be covered by their customers' disclosure duties and could trigger ineligibility for a prime contractor.

industries.industry: Agricultural employers using H-2A visa workers
industries.note: H-2A farmworker protections are on the disclosure list, but the bill only applies to USDA contractors, so the effect on most agricultural employers is limited.
